input.strategy_title: FIPS 140-3 compliance for the model serving stack
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Public-sector deals require the model serving stack to run on FIPS-enabled
OpenShift clusters using validated cryptographic modules. Today KServe
components and the serving data plane link non-validated crypto libraries in
several images, and we have no compliance evidence package. Certification
involves an external accredited laboratory (historical turnaround: six to nine
months) and mandatory security review board sign-off at defined milestones —
these human and third-party gates dominate the schedule regardless of
engineering speed.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | All serving-stack images run correctly on FIPS-enabled clusters using validated crypto modules (no non-validated crypto in the request path). |
| HLR-2 | P0 | A compliance evidence package (module inventory, build attestations, test results) is assembled and submitted through the security review board to the external certification lab. |
| HLR-3 | P1 | CI enforces FIPS regressions: a gating check fails any serving-stack build that reintroduces non-validated crypto usage. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Documentation states the FIPS support posture and cluster prerequisites. |

## Affected Components

- KServe
- Platform Operator

## Out of Scope

- FIPS posture for workbenches, pipelines, and training (separate strategies)
- Common Criteria certification

## Open Questions

None on scope — but note that lab scheduling and review-board cadence are
externally controlled and cannot be compressed by engineering effort.

# KServe image FIPS crypto remediation

## Description

Makes the KServe serving-stack images run correctly on FIPS-enabled OpenShift
clusters using validated cryptographic modules, with no non-validated crypto in
the inference request path. This epic delivers the audit of KServe images for
non-validated cryptographic library usage and the remediation of every finding,
plus the evidence artifacts (module inventory, build attestations, test
results) needed downstream for compliance certification.

## Scope

- Audit all KServe component images for non-validated cryptographic library
  usage — direct and transitive dependencies, statically and dynamically linked
  — and produce the KServe portion of the module inventory.
- Replace every non-validated crypto library used in the request path with a
  validated cryptographic module.
- Verify that inference serving works correctly on a FIPS-enabled OpenShift
  cluster in both serverless and raw deployment modes.
- Capture build attestations and test results from the remediated images in a
  form the compliance evidence package can consume.
- Incidental reference updates in build configuration that fall out of the
  library replacement are included here (no new documentation content).

## Acceptance Criteria

- The image audit produces a complete inventory of cryptographic modules linked
  into each KServe image, and every module used in the request path is a
  validated module.
- All remediated KServe images build green in the existing build pipeline.
- Inference requests succeed on a FIPS-enabled OpenShift cluster in both
  serverless and raw deployment modes, with no non-validated crypto invoked in
  the request path, as verified by test results retained for the compliance
  evidence package.
- The module inventory, build attestations, and test results for the KServe
  images are handed over in a consumable form for the compliance evidence
  package.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): all serving-stack images run correctly on FIPS-enabled clusters
  using validated crypto modules — KServe portion.

## Risks / Notes

- The volume of affected images and call sites is unknown until the audit runs
  ("several images" per the strategy). If the audit finds materially more
  images or crypto call sites than a single sprint can absorb, the epic should
  be re-split by image group or sub-system (see the decomposition summary's
  re-split trigger).

# CI FIPS regression gate for serving-stack builds

## Description

A gating CI check that fails any serving-stack build which reintroduces
non-validated cryptographic usage, so FIPS compliance cannot regress silently
after the initial remediation.

## Scope

- Implement a check that detects non-validated crypto usage in serving-stack
  build artifacts and images.
- Wire the check as a gating (merge/release-blocking) check in the KServe build
  pipeline and in the Platform Operator build pipeline — one logical change,
  one detection recipe, applied to every serving-stack build.
- The detection rules must cover the non-validated crypto usage patterns
  identified by the serving-stack image audits (the check's detection set is
  complete relative to those findings).
- Coordination with the remediation work is a content hand-off (the audit's
  findings feed the detection rules), not a start-stop dependency: the check
  can be built and validated against known patterns while remediation is in
  flight.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A build that reintroduces a known non-validated crypto usage pattern fails
  the gating check — verified with a deliberate positive-control violation in
  a test build.
- A clean, remediated build passes the check.
- The check is gating (it blocks merge or release) in both the KServe and the
  Platform Operator build pipelines.
- The check's detection rules cover the non-validated crypto usage patterns
  identified by the serving-stack image audits.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): CI enforces FIPS regressions — a gating check fails any
  serving-stack build that reintroduces non-validated crypto usage.

## Risks / Notes

- The epic is owned by RHOAI Serving but includes wiring the platform operator
  build pipeline; that wiring requires coordination with (or hand-off to) the
  pipeline's owners. If strict team ownership is preferred, the platform
  operator wiring can move into the platform operator remediation epic as an
  acceptance criterion without changing HLR coverage.

# FIPS compliance evidence package and certification submission

## Description

Assembles the FIPS 140-3 compliance evidence package for the model serving
stack — module inventory, build attestations, and test results — and submits
it through the security review board to the external accredited certification
laboratory, driving the submission through board sign-off and lab triage.

## Scope

- Assemble the complete module inventory across all serving-stack images in
  scope (KServe components, Platform Operator, and the serving data plane),
  consolidating the inventories produced by the remediation work.
- Collect the build attestations and FIPS test results produced for the
  remediated images.
- Package the evidence according to the security review board's and the
  certification lab's submission requirements.
- Submit the package through the security review board sign-off milestones to
  the external certification lab, and triage the lab's findings and feedback.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The evidence package contains the complete module inventory, build
  attestations, and test results for every serving-stack image in scope, and
  each entry is traceable to the image and build that produced it.
- The package is submitted through the security review board to the external
  certification lab, and the complete submitted package — contents, board
  sign-off records, and submission record — is archived and traceable to this
  epic's deliverable.
- Every security review board sign-off milestone defined for this submission
  is met and recorded in the package.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): a compliance evidence package (module inventory, build
  attestations, test results) is assembled and submitted through the security
  review board to the external certification lab.

## Risks / Notes

- The certification lab turnaround is historically six to nine months, and the
  review board meets on its own cadence; both are externally controlled and
  cannot be compressed by engineering effort. The acceptance criteria are
  deliberately set at the engineering completion point — the package submitted
  — not at the certificate being granted, whose timing is outside this epic's
  control.
- Lab triage — the lab's acknowledgment of the submission and the opening of a
  findings/response cycle — is the external lab's action, not this epic's
  deliverable. It is tracked here as an outcome (and drives any follow-up
  response work) rather than as an acceptance criterion, consistent with
  treating the certificate itself as outside this epic's control.
- The security review board sign-off and the lab submission are mandatory
  human and third-party process gates.

# FIPS support posture documentation

## Description

Documentation stating the FIPS support posture of the model serving stack and
the cluster prerequisites for running it on FIPS-enabled OpenShift, describing
what was actually built and enforced.

## Scope

Content outline:

- FIPS support posture of the serving stack: what is supported, at what
  maturity, and what is not in scope (workbenches, pipelines, training, and
  Common Criteria certification are out of scope per the strategy).
- Cluster prerequisites: FIPS-enabled OpenShift clusters, validated
  cryptographic module requirements, and deployment-mode considerations
  (serverless vs. raw deployment) relevant to FIPS operation.
- The CI enforcement posture: how the gating check prevents FIPS regressions
  in serving-stack builds and what a failed build means for consumers.
- References to the compliance evidence package and certification submission
  state where useful to consumers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Documentation topics stating the FIPS support posture and cluster
  prerequisites are published.
- The content is technically reviewed against the implemented remediation and
  CI enforcement, with the review sign-off recorded.
- Accuracy is validated against the architecture context and the implemented
  behavior (deployment modes, prerequisites, and enforcement behavior match
  what ships).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P2): documentation states the FIPS support posture and cluster
  prerequisites.

  change wired into both the KServe and the platform operator build pipelines.
  The epic is owned by RHOAI Serving; wiring the platform operator pipeline
  requires coordination with (or hand-off to) that pipeline's owners. If the
  teams prefer strict ownership, the platform-operator wiring can move into the
  platform operator remediation epic as an acceptance criterion without changing

- **Planning note (epic size)**: the KServe remediation epic's volume is unknown

  **Re-split trigger**: re-split this epic by image group or sub-system if the
